description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
The implementation of the TMT “Towards climate adaptation in Cuba: Strengthening capacities in multi hazard flood assessment and multi-functional solutions to minimize risk along the “Malecon” Area in Havana “ was fully achieved. The objectives were fully met and based on the feedback provided by the participants 100% considered that the course was between very good and good. The TMT was delivered by implementing 3 modules. All the modules were delivered face to face at the premises of INRH. The methodology used in the training consisted of a mix of lectures, teaching material, readings, power point slides, software manuals and guidelines, software tools (for example each participant were given a license of ArcGIS valid for one year), case studies (a mix of cases were used including case studies from the region), individual project and presentation as well as group discussion and feedback.
The three modules can be summarized as follows:
Module I: Methods and tools for understanding urban flood hazards due to intense precipitation, Urban drainage. Date: March 21-25, 2022. Modality: Face to face.
The module included lectures with theoretical explanation and concepts as a foundational knowledge for modelling and understanding of urban floods. Several topics were introduced and discussed related to urban hydrological processes, climate change and effects of urbanization. Several practices and exercises were don in Arcgis for the preprocessing od digital terrain data for modelling purposes and for coupling 2D flood models. For the use of computer modelling tools the online computer labs platform of IHE Delft was used. The practical exercises of the module include real case studies using the tools ArGIS and Mike Urban. Tools that are powerful to graphically display and present the results of the models, to enhance the understating of the problem and to facilitate decision making. Calibration was also discussed and there was a practical exercise were participants had the opportunity to manually adjust model parameters to fit measured time series data. During this module there were also online lectures from Delft, as one of the lecturers was not able to travel due to Covid19 regulations. Modules II and III were exchange in time due to limitations caused by the war in Ukraine the cost of the airfare tickets was really high. The initially planned module III was delivered in the second position in June and the initial planned module II was the last one and it was delivered in July 2022 in mutual agreement with the requesting organization.
Module II: Flood risk assessment and multifunctional solutions (NBS, Eng, Struct, Non Struct, etc). Date: June 6-10, 2022. Modality: Face to face.
During this module we connected the practical exercises of the first module with the theoretical background and concepts of flood risk assessment including flood hazards and vulnerability. The practical exercises were done using ArcGIS for the production of maps related to flood hazard, vulnerability and flood risk maps as well as cost and damages estimation. The analysis allowed the participants not only to exercise and practice what was discussed in class but also to understand the problem and the multiple consequences around urban floods
During this module nature-based solutions were also addressed as mitigation measures for floods and also as a strategy for climate change adaptation. Sustainable drainage systems were also discussed as multi-functional measures for drainage systems. As part of this topic each participant dedicated time to study one measure and produce a poster. Then in plenary each student explained the main issues, benefits, multi-functionality, costs and performance. There was space for questions, discussion and feedback. For the selection of multiple measures several tools were introduced and used for example the selection tool being developed as part of the Reconect project ([www.reconect.eu](http://www.reconect.eu/)) but also the climateapp.nl tool developed by Deltares. The output of this tools was used in another exercise for multi-criteria analysis for ranking different NBS measures according with some criteria and stakeholders’ preferences. The last part of the module connected the output of the previous tools for model the performance of some of the NBS measures using SWMM in two case studies in Colombia. One of these case studies was directly explained by one of IHE’s alumni in EPM, Medellin, The participants liked the interaction with other professional and similar case study form the region. This practical exercise was appreciated by the participants as it provides the opportunity to exchange knowledge and experiences, to learn from similar situations and experiences and as an effective way to share knowledge.
Module III: Understanding climate related risk in coastal cities: Methods and tools for the analysis of climate scenarios and sea level rise. Date: July 11-15, 2022. Modality: Face to face.
This module started with the basic principles of coastal engineering which were then connected with practical exercises that were developed using different tools such as Delft3D-FM to generate grids and bathymetries, to model waves the software Delft3D Wave was used. The practical exercise in this module was developed in groups to practice with the different tools that were presented during the module (Xbeach, SFINCS, Delft3D-Wave). The case study area used in this part of the course was the area around the Havana’s Malecon. Different solutions/measures were study to mitigate the flood effects or impacts in the Malecon area. Each group prepared a presentation for the plenary session were all the solutions and considerations were discussed and feedback was provided for each group and each of the tools and approaches used during the exercise.
